extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and courts/practitioners interpreting historic U.S. patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Statutory requirements and procedural rules for obtaining, defending, and enforcing U.S. patents under early Acts (1790–1832), including specification content, oaths, models, fees, remedies, challenges, arbitration for interfering applications, court jurisdiction, and renewal procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must be 'clearly, truly, and fully' (1790)
rubrics_metrics.description: The letters-patent shall describe the said invention or discovery, clearly, truly, and fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1 (1790) requires the patent to recite the petition's allegations and to describe the invention 'clearly, truly, and fully' as part of the grant process (certified by Attorney-General and recorded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification particularity and enablement (1790/1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification in writing, containing a description, accompanied with drafts or models... shall be so particular, and said models so exact, as not only to distinguish the invention from other things before known and used, but also to enable a workman or other person skilled in the art... to make, construct, or use the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 2 (1790) and 3 (1793) impose an early written-description/enablement requirement: the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the invention, and where drawings/models are appropriate they must be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor's oath/affirmation of being true inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Every inventor, before he can receive his patent, shall swear or affirm that he does verily believe that he is the true inventor or discoverer of the art, machine, or improvement for which he solicits a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3 (1793) requires an oath/affirmation (made before an authorized officer) that the applicant believes himself the true inventor; similar attestations appear in other acts; false statements could render a patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings, written references, and specimens where nature admits
rubrics_metrics.description: He shall accompany the whole with drawings and written references, where the nature of the case admits of drawings, or with specimens of the ingredients, and of the composition of matter, sufficient in quantity for the purpose of experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3 (1793) mandates drawings/references for machines and specimens for compositions of matter when appropriate; the description must explain the principle and several modes of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models may be required by Secretary
rubrics_metrics.description: Such inventor shall, moreover, deliver a model of his machine, provided the Secretary shall deem such model to be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3 (1793) and earlier provisions allow the patent office official to require physical models when necessary to the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term limited to fourteen years
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants a term not exceeding fourteen years for the sole and exclusive right to make, construct, use, and vend the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set out in Sections 1 (1790) and 1 (1793): the statutory patent term was capped at 14 years under these early acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney-General examination and certification within 15 days
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent delivered to the Attorney-General to be examined; who, within fifteen days after delivery, if he shall find the same conformable to this act, shall certify accordingly at the foot thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 1 (1790) and 1 (1793) require a prompt examination/certification step by the Attorney-General as part of issuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary must furnish copies and permit making models (public access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon application... for a copy of any such specification, and for permission to have similar model or models made, it shall be the duty of the Secretary to give such a copy, and to permit the person so applying... to take, or make... at the expense of such applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 3 (1790) provides public access to specifications and models on request (at applicant's expense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement remedies — jury-assessed damages and forfeiture (1790)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person so offending shall forfeit and pay to the said patentee... such damages as shall be assessed by a jury, and moreover shall forfeit to the person aggrieved, the thing or things so devised, made, constructed, used, employed, or vended... which may be recovered in an action on the case founded on this act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 4 (1790) provides both monetary damages (jury-assessed) and recovery/forfeiture of infringing articles as remedies for unauthorized use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treble or multiple damages penalties (1793/1800)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1793: Every person so offending shall forfeit and pay... a sum that shall be at least equal to three times the price for which the patentee has usually sold or licensed the use of the said invention. 1800: Offender shall forfeit and pay a sum equal to three times the actual damage sustained by such patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections in the 1793 and 1800 Acts impose enhanced (three-times) monetary penalties for infringement; the precise measure varies (three times usual sale/license price vs. three times actual damages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents and specifications prima facie evidence; defenses of insufficiency or fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: The said patents or specifications shall be prima facie evidence that the said patentee was the first and true inventor... but the defendant may plead the general issue, and give... evidence... that the specification does not contain the whole of the truth... or contains more than is necessary... and if the concealment of part, or the addition of more than is necessary, shall appear to have been intended to mislead, or shall actually mislead the public... the verdict and judgment shall be for the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 6 (1790) and 6 (1793) establish the evidentiary effect of filed specifications but preserve defenses: lack of enablement/full disclosure, overclaiming, intent to mislead, prior use or prior description, and surreptitious procurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-limited post-issuance challenge for surreptitious/false patents (1790 & 1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1790: Upon oath... motion made... within one year after issuing the said patent... judge may grant rule to show cause and potentially repeal the patent. 1793: Similar motion may be made within three years after issuing the said patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 5 (1790) and 10 (1793) provide procedures and statutory time windows (initially one year, later three years) for challenging patents alleged to have been obtained surreptitiously or by false suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interfering applications submitted to arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of interfering applications, the same shall be submitted to the arbitration of three persons, one chosen by each applicant, and the third appointed by the Secretary of State; decision signed by any two shall be final as to granting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 9 (1793) prescribes mandatory arbitration among applicants with competing claims to the same invention; refusal to appoint an arbitrator results in grant to the opposite party; Secretary may appoint when applicants do not agree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment recording and assignee rights
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be lawful for any inventor... to assign the title and interest in the said invention at any time, and the assignee, having recorded the said assignment in the office of the Secretary of State, shall thereafter stand in the place of the original inventor, both as to right and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 4 (1793) requires recording assignments in the Secretary's office to effect substitution of assignee's rights and responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aliens eligible after two years' residence; oath about prior foreign use (1800)
rubrics_metrics.description: All rights... shall be extended to all aliens who at the time of petitioning shall have resided for two years within the United States; provided every person petitioning shall make oath that such invention hath not, to the best of his knowledge, been known or used either in this or any foreign country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1 (1800) opened patent privileges to resident aliens (subject to a two-year residency) but required an oath against prior known/used status; patents later shown previously known/used are void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to apply survives inventor's death (1800)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where any person hath made any new invention... and shall have died before any patent shall be granted therefor, the right of applying for and obtaining such patent shall devolve on the legal representatives of such person in trust for heirs or devisees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2 (1800) provides that legal representatives may pursue patents on behalf of a deceased inventor, with adapted oath language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit courts have original cognizance and equity powers (1819)
rubrics_metrics.description: The circuit courts of the United States shall have original cognizance, as well in equity as at law, of all actions, suits, controversies, and cases arising under any law... granting exclusive rights to inventors; and upon any bill in equity... shall have authority to grant injunctions according to the course and principles of courts of equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section (1819) extends jurisdiction of federal circuit courts to patent cases and expressly authorizes equitable remedies (injunctions) on appropriate terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary to publish list of expired patents annually (1832)
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be the duty of the Secretary of State, annually, in the month of January, to report to Congress, and to publish in two Washington newspapers, a list of all the patents... which shall have expired within the year immediately preceding, with the names of the patentees, alphabetically arranged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1 (1832) requires publication and reporting of patents that have expired during the previous year for public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition to Congress to prolong/renew patent term (1832) — notice and evidentiary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Application to Congress to prolong or renew the term of a patent shall be made before its expiration, and shall be notified at least once a month, for three months before its presentation, in two Washington newspapers and in one newspaper of the State where the patentee resides; the petition shall set forth the grounds, be verified by oath; evidence in its support may be taken before any judge or justice of the peace; it shall be accompanied by a statement of the ascertained value of the discovery, and of the receipts and expenditures of the patentee, so as to exhibit the profit or loss arising therefrom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2 (1832) prescribes strict timing, publication/notice, oath/verification, and documentary/evidentiary support (value, receipts/expenditures) for Congressional extension/renewal petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees and cost schedule for filing and copies (1790 & 1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1790: fees such as petition filing fifty cents; filing specifications ten cents per 100 words; making out patent two dollars; affixing great seal one dollar; indorsing delivery day twenty cents. 1793/1794/1793 variants: inventors shall pay thirty dollars into the treasury at petition time; copy fees at twenty cents per 100 words, drawings $2 per copy, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 7 (1790) and 11 (1793) set out fees payable at various stages (filing petition, specification copies, drawings), including a lump-sum payment in 1793 to cover clerk-hire; copy/drawing fees are separately charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim/procedural restoration of suits after repeal (1794)
rubrics_metrics.description: All suits, actions, process and proceedings heretofore had in any District Court under the 1790 act which may have been set aside, suspended or abated by reason of the repeal of that act may be restored, at the instance of the plaintiff or defendant, within one year from the passing of this act, to the same situation in which they were when set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1794 supplementary act allows reinstatement of pending litigation affected by statutory repeal, with procedures for bringing parties into court before further orders are entered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition that mere change of form or proportions is not a discovery (1793)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hereby enacted and declared, that simply changing the form or the proportions of any machine, or composition of matter, in any degree, shall not be deemed a discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2 (1793) clarifies that trivial alterations of form/proportion do not qualify as patentable discoveries; substantive improvement is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary and exception practice for master's reports (equity/profits context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complainants' exceptions to a master's report: (1) exceptions stating evidence proving larger profits or larger damages must be supported by references to the particular evidence relied upon; (2) exceptions stating master erred in admitting inadmissible evidence must cite the particular evidence improperly admitted; draft-report exceptions must reference particular evidence; final-report exceptions must be supported by references to evidence or by special statements of the master enabling avoidance of that necessity; master's conclusions stand unless clearly erroneous; draft report should contain conclusions alone; final report final conclusions plus statements of fact and evidence parties lawfully require attached; where master receives no direction to report evidence his report contains nothing but his finding, and his finding is conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections §749–§750 (profits/chancery practice) prescribe how exceptions to a master's report must be supported, what to include in draft and final reports, when evidence must accompany reports, and the deference courts give to masters' findings (stand unless clearly erroneous). These rules govern how parties must present or preserve challenges to masters' factual determinations (relevant in patent accounting/litigation).
